title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork

reading.body:
A class-action lawsuit alleges that Oura's smart rings cannot accurately detect sleep stages as advertised, despite their $300-plus price point. The suit claims the device's algorithms and sensors cannot measure the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep tracking and instead rely on unreliable artificial intelligence. This is a model deployed in a consumer product making claims about its own accuracy that users relied on to make a purchase decision.

Oura disputes the allegations and cites independent peer-reviewed studies supporting its sleep staging accuracy, noting the rings have been validated against polysomnography, the clinical standard. It is not established whether the company's claims were false, whether the validation studies actually support the claimed accuracy, or what independent testing would show about the device's performance in real-world conditions.

reports.title: Oura, Smart Ring Maker, Sued for Alleged False Claims and Unreliable AI
Oura faces lawsuit accusing it of misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy

summary:
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring company, alleging false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. Filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco on Thursday, the suit claims that Oura's rings, priced at $300 and up, cannot accurately detect sleep stages as advertised. The lawsuit argues that Oura's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to measure the physiological signals necessary for accurate sleep tracking and instead rely on unreliable artificial intelligence, comparing the results to guessing.

Oura disputes the allegations, stating it stands behind its scientific claims and noting that independent peer-reviewed studies support its sleep staging accuracy. The company maintains that while its rings are not medical devices, they have been validated against polysomnography, the clinical standard for sleep studies. This represents the second lawsuit against Oura, as another ongoing class action alleges the company collected personal information without customer consent for two years. The case will seek jury trial status and class action certification, though it remains unclear whether current buyers can join the suit or what compensation may result.
